en: The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom Spoken by the Buddha, in one fascicle;
translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, together with [the assembly].

He was accompanied by a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as forty billion bodhisattvas. All had attained dharanis; all had attained all samādhis; all had realized the dharma of emptiness; all had attained the state of quiescent non-conceptualization; all had attained immovable vows; all had attained the practice of the dharani of non-attachment; and they had attained countless gateways to dharanis.

At that time, the Buddha entered a samādhi-samāpatti; he was suddenly formless, invisible, and ungraspable. Like space, he was unknowable, non-abiding, unobtainable, without self, without action, without coming, without going, not abiding, not ceasing, not paired, not unpaired, not body, not sorrow, not joy, not mind, not non-conforming to the mind, not the sphere of speech, nor was there this emptiness of speech, and he was without attachment.
At that time, the Buddha entered this samādhi-samāpatti; consequently, the body of the Buddha could no longer be seen, nor could it be conceived of.

Neither the body of the Buddha, nor his mind, nor his thought could be conceived of. Furthermore, neither the inner robe, the outer robe, nor the seat could be seen, nor could he be seen when walking in meditation, nor was there even any sound.

At that time, the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi illuminated the suns and moons of the trichiliocosm; consequently, the light of all the suns and moons within the Buddha-fields of the trichiliocosm was completely eclipsed and could no longer be seen.

The radiance of all *maṇi* jewels, *vaiḍūrya* jewels, the various heavens and celestial thrones, and the renowned incenses of Śakra and Brahmā were all extinguished, for they were all obscured and hidden by the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi. Within the trichiliocosm, only the fragrance of this samādhi was perceived.

It illuminated the various Buddha-fields, such that the eyes of the people therein were no longer obstructed by the Cakravāḍa mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa mountains, Mount Sumeru, or the various Black Mountains.
At that time, canopies of the seven treasures appeared, covering the trichiliocosm.
All the Buddha-fields, as well as the Bamboo Grove and Vulture Peak Mountain, were completely filled with various kinds of flowers.
The ground is entirely level, and from the earth grow lotus flowers.
Each flower is as large as a chariot wheel;
a single flower has one hundred thousand petals.
Upon each of those flowers were canopies made of the seven treasures.
The ground throughout the realm of Magadha became as soft as celestial silk.

Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction dispatched countless bodhisattvas in their final birth before enlightenment, commanding them to arrive at the Sahāloka buddha-field:
“There is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni, who currently resides within the realm of all Buddhas, having deeply entered the Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā-samādhi-samāpatti.”
If there is a bodhisattva who accumulates merit and practices the six pāramitās for a hundred kalpas without employing upāyakauśalya, it would not equal hearing this samādhi even once.

The bodhisattvas immediately accepted the Buddha’s instruction; by means of their supernormal powers, they flew to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated before the Buddha, and all withdrew to sit upon lotus flowers.
In this way, the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the southern direction likewise dispatched countless bodhisattvas.

From the western, northern, southeastern, southwestern, northwestern, northeastern, upper, and lower directions—each of these Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, also dispatched countless bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) to the Sahāloka realm, saying:
"There is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni, who currently dwells within the sphere of all Buddhas, deeply entered into the *samādhi* of the Seal of the Wisdom of the Tathāgata."
If there is a bodhisattva who accumulates merit and practices the six pāramitās for a hundred kalpas without employing upāyakauśalya, it would not equal hearing this samādhi but once.

The bodhisattvas immediately accepted the Buddha’s instruction; using their supernormal powers, they flew to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated before the Buddha, and all withdrew to sit upon lotus flowers.
At that time, from all distant regions throughout this trichiliocosm, the assembly of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas all came together at the Bamboo Grove to stand before the Buddha.
At that time, incalculable bodhisattvas and forty billion bhikṣus and bodhisattvas all came together at the Bamboo Grove.

By the majestic power of this samādhi, the Śakras, the Brahmās, the Maheśvaras, the Śubhakṛtsnas, and all the dragon kings, the yakṣa kings, the gandharva kings, the asura kings, the garuḍa kings, the kiṃnara kings, and the mahoraga kings—all these kings, each accompanied by their own incalculable retinues—came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, throughout this trichiliocosm, from the lowest realms up to the twenty-eighth heaven, including all devas, humans, and non-humans, there was no empty space left; they were entirely and completely filled.
The Venerable disciples Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Kauṣṭhila-Kātyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and others immediately went before Mañjuśrī and asked him, saying:
"The Buddha’s previous samādhi and samāpatti are now no longer seen; we do not know the place to which he has gone."
“We pray that you will explain this for us!
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:

“Virtuous one, you are fully endowed with wisdom; why do you not each, through your respective samādhis, search together through countless Buddha-fields to know what the Buddha’s body is like and how it acts?”

Immediately, Śāriputra and the others each entered their own samādhi and searched together through incalculable Buddha-fields; yet they could not see the Buddha’s body at all, nor did they know the place where he had gone.
Śāriputra and the others immediately arose from their samādhi and again approached Mañjuśrī, asking:
"We have each used our respective samādhis to search through countless Buddha-fields, yet we have neither seen the Buddha-body nor known where it has gone."
"I wish to hear and know it; please explain it for me!
Mañjuśrī said, "Venerable Śāriputra and the others, you who do not know where the Buddha has gone, all sit down in peace for now."
"The Buddha shall return of his own accord in a mere moment.
At that time, the Buddha arose from the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom and immediately shook the trichiliocosm Buddha-field.
Śāriputra and the others then stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what samādhi does the Buddha abide?
We have searched for the Buddha with our eyes of wisdom, yet none among us is able to know his location.
The Buddha spoke to Śāriputra, saying:
“The places where the Buddha arrives cannot be known by Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and the like;
only the Buddha knows them himself. Why is this so?
Because it is without thought, unmoving, and unshakable. "Śāriputra,
there are one hundred and sixty-two matters concerning the Buddha’s body that are difficult to comprehend."
What are these one hundred and sixty-two matters?

They are: not the body, non-action, non-arising, non-decrease, never having existed, incomparable, having nothing with which to be compared, without movement, without destination, unknowable, and furthermore, non-existent.
It is practiced as all-purity; it is non-existent, neither being nor non-being;
it does not proceed, nor does it abide; it is neither born, nor received, nor heard, nor seen, nor smelled, nor tasted, nor touched;
it has no departure or inquiry, and no return or response.
It is neither an inquiry nor a response; it is neither mind nor thought; it is neither the mind nor the thoughts of the mind, being detached from such things as the mind and its thoughts.
The mind has nothing with which to be compared, nothing with which to be associated;
it comes not and goes not. It is neither moistening nor cleansing; it does not exist again; it is neither fear nor dread.
It is neither moving nor shaking; it is without creation and without accomplishment;
it is neither full nor not full; it is neither seeing nor clarity, neither non-clarity nor darkness, neither non-darkness;
it is neither cessation, for it is already free from cessation, and it is pure within cessation.
Furthermore, it is utterly pure; it is non-existent regarding form, free from craving, and entirely without self.
It is detached from what is not-self, abiding in non-abiding, neither having a location nor a source, yet not being without a source.
It is neither a phenomenon (*dharma*), nor is it a non-phenomenon; it is neither a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), nor is it not...
It is not a field of merit, nor is it exhaustion, nor is it that which can be exhausted; it is non-existent, yet detached from non-existence;
it is removed from words, removed from sounds, removed from teachings, removed from practice, and removed from recollection;
it is neither calamity nor the absence of calamity, and it is immeasurable.
It is neither non-measurement, nor coming, nor going; neither dual, nor non-dual;
neither dependent, nor non-dependent; neither characterized, nor uncharacterized; it is without characteristics yet capable of manifesting characteristics;
it is without the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and is neither attached nor free from all attachments.
Causing all people to attain faith; neither receiving nor entering into abiding; regarding each truth and further truth;
transcending all that is not-self; there is nothing to be transcended; purity with nothing to be purified; crossing over calamities and hardships as having nothing to be crossed over;
what is spoken and what is not spoken—these two are equal and without distinction; in equality there is no equality; immeasurable.
Equal to the equal, equal to emptiness, equal to the non-abiding, equal to the unarisen, and equal to the unattainable;
that which is established is without anything to be established; it is tranquil and yet further tranquil; it is luminous within the tranquil and luminous;
it does not turn within practice, yet it can turn practice; it severs all attachments; all dharmas are truly non-dual from the very beginning.
It has come from nowhere and possesses nothing; that which is to be awakened has already been truly awakened.
It has transcended all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and in that which is transcended by these phenomena, there is nothing further to transcend.
It is neither "is" nor "is not," neither long nor short, neither round nor square, neither body nor substance.
It is neither an entrance, nor is there anything entered; it is neither the world, nor that which belongs to the world;
it has never been seen by anyone, nor has it ever been known by anyone; it is neither departing, nor is it not departing;
it is neither caused by worldly conditions, nor is it not caused by worldly conditions. Thus, this body is ungraspable.
It is neither attainment, nor existence, nor non-existence; it neither goes nor comes;
it is neither mental conception, nor sorrow, nor action, nor non-action;
it is neither contention, nor non-contention; it is neither nirvāṇa, nor non-nirvāṇa; nor is it...
"It is neither practicing nor not practicing.
These constitute the one hundred and sixty-two matters.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“The Buddha-body is thus.
Even if one desires to perceive the Buddha-body through conceptual thought, no one is able to see it. Why is this so?
"The Buddha-body cannot be perceived or known through conceptualization.
At that time, the Buddha, wishing to seal the Great Wisdom with the Samādhi of Vastness throughout the ten directions, spoke these verses:
"This body is also not a body; It has already attained liberation from the body."
There is neither action nor existence, and even destruction is unattainable.
The characteristics of all phenomena are both dual and not dual;
those who wish to see the bodies of the Buddhas will find that their abodes are likewise thus.
Neither is it non-existent nor is it not non-existent;
It is neither sorrowful nor free from sorrow. Neither grasping nor relinquishing, Neither equal nor long, Neither delighting nor abiding— All things arise from nowhere.
The Buddha’s body is already thus, and he is therefore able to bring about peace and security.
It is not something that can be produced, nor is it impossible; one attains emptiness and is free from conceptualization.
It is neither form nor mind, nor is it non-existent; there is no self, nor is it a single entity.
In sensation there is no sensing; in existence there is nothing existing.
Such is the true nature of the body of all the Perfectly Awakened Ones:
neither rigid nor weak, without flaw and without impurity.
Neither interrupted nor continuous, neither existent nor destroyed;
there is nothing to be obtained therein, neither more nor less, and nothing lost.
Those who wish to see the bodies of all Buddhas will find them entirely free from dust and defilement.
Neither seen nor heard, neither fragrant nor possessing tactile qualities,
neither known nor moved— like a shadow that dwells upon all forms,
it awakens the minds of those attached to the world.
The Buddha has already perfected his body; all things are likewise so.
It is neither body nor substance, neither equality nor truth;
it is neither pure nor impure, for the sense faculties do not exist therein.
Neither hidden nor not hidden, like the moon in water;
if one wishes to see the bodies of all Buddhas, they are all exactly thus.
Body follows upon body, for causes and conditions are fundamentally natural.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going;
not seen within the triple world, yet appearing like a magical illusion.
Those who wish to see the bodies of all Buddhas will find them neither moving nor wavering.
Neither sound nor dispute, neither silence nor stillness;
Not attained, never existing, neither present nor absent.
Like the primordial nature of space, Spontaneously devoid of anything at all.
Having seen the Buddha in this manner, one should make offerings day and night.
Even if all the billion-fold buddha-fields throughout the ten directions,
reaching up to the twenty-eighth heaven, were filled with every kind of precious jewel, [it would not equal the merit of such an offering].
To make offerings to the Buddhas in this manner for even countless eons is not equal to copying this sutra;
its merit surpasses that of the former.
It is as if, for twice as many countless eons as there are grains of sand along the Ganges, one were to offer such worship.
Circulating within this state, one may constantly practice a mind of equanimous compassion;
yet it does not equal the clear understanding of wisdom that realizes this Seal Samādhi.
Though one were to do so for countless years, its merit would still surpass the former.
If one were to wander through the five realms of existence for countless eons,
enduring all such hardships throughout those many kalpas,
it would not equal the wisdom of a single moment that understands this Seal Samādhi.
That merit is like a mustard seed placed beside Mount Sumeru.
If a person within the triple world, from birth until they have grown to full stature, were to carry all such beings upon their head and endure this for incalculable eons;
[their merit would still not equal that of one who hears this Dharma].
Their bodies do not grow weary, nor do they engage in strenuous toil;
though they are able to endure all such things, it is not equal to understanding samādhi.
Suppose one were born throughout the entire universe, and for many more kalpas than that.
If all the grains of sand in a hundred kalpas were used as a count,
it would not equal the power of a single day and night spent practicing this Seal Samādhi.
Should one wish to compare its merit, it cannot be matched by mere wisdom.
One who possesses such wisdom always acts in accordance with its characteristics;
throughout incalculable eons, this is compared to but a single speck of dust.
One who can clearly and thoroughly understand this is the one who possesses the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom.
If one were to compare that merit, it would be like taking a single drop from the ocean.
Do not rely on physical marks and signs, nor seek to see the Buddha through conceptual visualization.
Do not be like those attached to existence who wish to see the Tathāgata.
As Subhūti has seen it, so is he who sees the Buddha;
having thus seen the Buddha, there is no three-thousandfold world-system at all. "So it is, Śāriputra!"

The Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā-samādhi: when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are unimpeded throughout the ten directions and desire to see all Buddhas, they should direct their innermost intent and practice this samādhi day and night. They will then behold the countless samādhi-gates practiced by all the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, abiding in the dharma of non-obstruction. This is the gate of reliance for dhāraṇī; from within this, one perfects the primary marks (lakṣaṇa), and from within this, one perfects the secondary refinements (anuvyañjana).
For one who practices in this way, all veils of sin are completely removed;
all demonic activities have been transcended;
and everything spoken by the Buddha is found to be precise and true.
The Buddha’s dwelling and his speech are without deficiency and are entirely complete;
his physical conduct is free from blemish;
and the conduct of his mental intentions is pure and stainless.

If one wishes to understand the conduct of the Buddhas, desires to comprehend the minds of all people so that each may find their proper place, and wishes to give rise to the vow to attain Buddhahood in a Buddha-field, one should practice this samādhi.

Those who wish to obtain the radiance from within the Buddha’s crown, those who wish to assemble the community of bhikṣus, and those who wish to adorn their buddha-field—those who desire sovereignty over what they seek and perform whatever actions they desire—should practice and uphold this samādhi.
Why is this so? It is like a medicinal tree, in whose presence everything one seeks is fully provided.
This samādhi is also like this; whatever a bodhisattva seeks within this samādhi is likewise fully provided.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
“Supreme wisdom is the king of wisdom; Wisdom can scatter all attachments to desire.
This honored wisdom enters the gateway of wisdom; This seal is the scripture of immeasurable wisdom.”
Knowing the faculties, conduct, abiding, and the ground of wisdom; with unimpeded wisdom, he dispels darkness;
with wisdom that eliminates attachment, he expounds the Dharma; his sutras shine like the sun upon the three realms.
Constantly practicing the samādhis of equanimity and so forth, all attachments are severed through the truths;
led by the seal of the wisdom of all samādhis, the Buddhas are of this very lineage.
Desiring to attain the perfection of jewels, may one possess the marks of merit and the power of divine feet;
whatever the mind aspires to shall be obtained from this—the joy of the Buddhas in this samādhi.
The King delighted in his kingdom and his ministers; he was the unsurpassed treasure, the Tathāgata.
With the defilements of lust and anger entirely eliminated, he preached this sutra through the power of the Jewel Samādhi.
Learn from me the meaning of reverence; Maintain purity and eliminate the notion of self.
The courageous one destroys birth and death, And by upholding the True Dharma, attains samādhi.
Wisdom can speak what ought to be spoken; by upholding this wisdom one gains great intelligence.
Wisdom can radiate light everywhere; this sutra is the gateway to wisdom.
They are able to completely subdue the self and exhaust the sixty-two kinds of doubt;
having reached the gate of the Buddha without fear, they are then endowed with these marks and signs of excellence.
Among the Three Honored Ones, the Buddha is the most honored; He alone can expound the seven factors of enlightenment.
To those who are indolent, he manifests the Dharma; This samādhi is inexhaustible.
All dharmas should be extensively expounded; entering the *anutpattika-dhāraṇī*, one upholds these dharmas and enters the ten directions. This *dhāraṇī* is like the ocean.
Within this, one accomplishes giving, as well as precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom;
these are inexhaustible, and by abiding in this sutra, one achieves the infinite.
Do not fear the ground of sinful karma, nor the various māras and evil realms;
practicing samādhi cannot be harmed, and one shall attain Buddhahood as originally vowed.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this Dharma, taking the ten directions as witness,
those who come seeking the vessel of the Dharma shall, by upholding this sutra, attain the abiding of the Dharma.
The sutras of the Buddhas of the past are the mother; those of the future likewise follow them;
the Buddhas of the present emerge from them; those who practice these are the children of the Buddha.
When the stains of transgression are removed and conduct no longer wavers, one transcends the seventh stage and proceeds toward the Dharma;
whoever abides in this sutra shall be fully endowed with the jewels of all Buddhas.
When this Dharma was being taught, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of thirty Ganges Rivers all attained this samādhi.
Sixty-eight nayuta-koti of bodhisattvas had all their karmic obstructions removed and were established in the stage of *avaivartika*; they all attained the inexhaustible *dhāraṇī* of entering sounds.

Six billion devas and humans, who from the very beginning had never once conceived the aspiration for bodhicitta, have now all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; having heard this samādhi, they all joyfully aspire to it.
Having made this aspiration, he shall thereafter abide on the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) and shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the Buddha immediately conferred upon him the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), saying: "After thirty billion hundred thousand kalpas, you shall all become Buddhas, named 'Free from Fear' (*Vīta-bhaya*)."
Each of the bodhisattvas gave rise to their own vows and immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thereafter, within those buddha-fields, they all became Buddhas, all bearing the same name.
At that time, the Buddha, having surveyed the entire assembly through samādhi, addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:

"For this reason, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva who wishes to protect my Dharma should abide in non-attachment; they should repent, uphold [the teachings], and expound them; they should always dwell in purity and solitude, and should not rely upon anything."
Mañjuśrī then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and prostrated himself with his head to the ground to pay homage to the Buddha. He addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I am able to endure and protect this Dharma of non-attachment; regarding the path of a bodhisattva, there is no ‘mine’ and no ‘self,’ it does not exist, nor has it ever existed; it is neither seen nor heard, neither attained nor lost.”
At that time, thirty billion bodhisattvas within the assembly all rose with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We are able to endure these countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas in order to protect the bodhisattva practice."
The various bodhisattvas each offered their upper robes as an offering to the Buddha and immediately made vows.
The Buddha spoke to Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"Mindful of your original vows and practices, you shall uphold this Dharma hereafter."
Among those thirty billion bodhisattvas, only eight thousand bodhisattvas were able to uphold this Dharma;
the remaining bodhisattvas were all stubborn and could not uphold the Dharma.
"In the future, they will all cause my Dharma to fall into disorder; yet they will neither feel remorse nor uphold it.
Maitreya! There are seven matters that give rise to the aspiration for bodhicitta."
What are these seven matters?
First, generating the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Second, when the Dharma is about to perish, protecting the Dharma so that it does not perish, thereby generating the aspiration for enlightenment.
Third, to give rise to compassion for humans and non-humans throughout the ten directions, and to give rise to the bodhisattva-mind.
Fourth, upon seeing a bodhisattva, to immediately give rise to the bodhisattva-mind.
Fifth, one gives rise to the bodhicitta through the act of giving.
Sixth, upon seeing others give rise to the bodhicitta, one emulates them and gives rise to the bodhicitta.
Seventh, upon hearing that the Buddha’s body possesses the thirty-two marks of excellence and is praised by people, one gives rise to the bodhicitta.
Maitreya! These are the seven matters.

One should give rise to the mind of a bodhisattva-tathāgata; one should protect the Dharma so that it does not perish; and one should arouse the bodhisattva-mind out of compassion for the people and non-humans of the ten directions. Those who possess these samādhis can protect the bodhisattva-mind and will swiftly attain *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
"Those among the four classes of followers who have resolved to attain the bodhisattva path are all 'sturdy' bodhisattvas.
The Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"If one abides in five dharmas, one will swiftly attain the stage of Avaivartika (non-retrogression)."
What are these five dharmas?
First, to maintain an impartial mind toward humans and non-humans throughout the ten directions.
Second, to harbor no feelings of favoritism or aversion regarding the wealth and treasures of others.
Third, when there are those who preach the Dharma of the sutras, one shall follow them even unto death and never speak ill of them.
Fourth, regarding offerings such as clothing, bedding, seats, sleeping requisites, or medicine for illness and infirmity—whatever is appropriate to receive—one shall have no attachment whatsoever.
Fifth, they enter deeply into the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
These are the five dharmas by which a bodhisattva dwelling therein knows the marks of an avaivartika bodhisattva.
“Furthermore, there are five qualities by which a bodhisattva dwelling [in this way] becomes stubborn and rigid. What are these five qualities?

First, his face lacks a healthy complexion; second, all his actions are timid and weak; third, he is stingy and greedy; fourth, he is deceitful and sycophantic; fifth, his mouth speaks only of emptiness.”
These are the five dharmas by which a bodhisattva abides in the state of being stubborn and rigid.
"Furthermore, there are five other dharmas by which a bodhisattva abides and knows that these are the dharmas of an avaivartika.
What are these five dharmas?
First, non-self; second, non-person; third, not abiding in the duality of dharmas; fourth, non-attachment to the bodhisattva; fifth, not maintaining the conceptualization of viewing the Buddha.
"These are the five dharmas by which a bodhisattva abides and swiftly attains *avaivartika* [irreversibility].
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"One should not be arrogant, Nor harbor jealousy, Nor falsely construct erroneous speech."
Those who seek out the faults of others, who do so not merely through speech, and who are timid and weak—
such persons as these are unable to protect the Dharma.
Dwelling in seclusion, they are able to endure what is subtle and profound;
not merely speaking with their mouths, they are like rhinoceroses, always delighting in solitude.
Those of such a kind can protect the Dharma for future generations.
Always delighting in solitude and finding joy in purity, like a frightened bird that finds refuge in the deep mountains;
not delighting in offerings, like the vast emptiness of space—such a person is able to protect the honored Dharma.
They cast away their bodies and even their lives, let alone all the precious treasures of the world;
exerting themselves with diligent effort and remaining unattached— such vessels of the Dharma are able to protect the future teaching.
In future ages, there will be such persons who will say of themselves, "I am a bodhisattva practicing the bodhisattva path.
Their resolve will be confused and they will be attached to the world; they will be unable to practice or protect the luminous Dharma.
At that time, after eighty billion kalpas had passed,
there was a Buddha named Prabhāsa who, for the sake of all people, preached this samādhi.
In the first great assembly, there were eighty nayutas; in the second assembly, sixty or seventy nayutas;
and in the third assembly, seventy-three nayutas—all of whom attained the stage of avaivartika.
The lifespan of that Buddha shall be ten million years; the light from his neck shall extend for seventy yojanas;
the number of bhikṣu monks shall be nine hundred and ninety million, all of whom have attained mastery and are arhats.
At that time there was a king, ruler of the people, named Hui-shang (Jñānottara), who was a Cakravartin.
At that time, the expanse of Jambudvīpa measured twenty thousand yojanas;
the four continents were all likewise in number.
The king had sixty billion court ladies, and his sons numbered one thousand, all fully complete;
the name of that land was Sukhāvatī, the Land of Utmost Bliss and No Weariness.
In the twenty thousand commanderies and counties, the people within the realm each have pleasure gardens where they constantly enjoy peace and security;
the five grains grow spontaneously, as if in the heavens,
such that there is nothing they lack.
At that time, the Honored King heard within a dream that there was a Buddha in the world named Prabhāsa.
Awakening from his dream, he went at once to the Buddha's abode, followed by sixty billion carriages of ministers and subordinates.
At that time, having heard from the Buddha this honored sutra, this subtle and wondrous samādhi,
the profound treasury of all Buddhas, he immediately offered up all his kingdoms to the Buddha;
whatever was required for offerings was provided without any deficiency.
In all lands, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, lecture halls were established using sandalwood;
in all these lecture halls, human offerings were provided,
and the grounds where they walked were spread with gold leaf, continuing thus for eighty-four thousand years.
He did not attend to royal affairs, but devoted himself solely to serving the Buddha;
he took no pleasure in sleep or reclining, but diligently served his Honored One; he did not engage in worldly matters, nor did he have any attachment to the kingdom.
Suppose there were someone who, speaking of the King’s virtues day after day,
could never reach the end of them;
the offerings made to the Buddha are likewise beyond measure.
Why is this? Desiring the samādhi, he immediately withdrew to dwell alone and reflected within himself:

All that the Buddha, the God among Gods, taught during that interval— the Dharma he proclaimed—
he received and accepted in its entirety.
In every kingdom and district, sixty-four billion stupas were erected;

The Buddha spoke to Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"If there is a bodhisattva who has already generated the bodhicitta before a hundred buddhas, yet subsequently ruins and destroys their bodhisattva practice;

or if there is a bodhisattva who has already generated the bodhicitta before a thousand buddhas, and then again generates the bodhicitta, but slanders the Vaipulya sutras and does not understand them;..."

If, after having already aroused the bodhicitta before one hundred thousand Buddhas, one subsequently arouses the bodhicitta again, yet does not revile the Vaipulya sutras, nor recites, reads, or studies them;

or if, after having already aroused the bodhicitta before one million Buddhas, one subsequently arouses the bodhicitta again, yet does not revile the Vaipulya sutras, nor recites, reads, or studies them;

or if, after having already aroused the bodhicitta before ten million Buddhas, one subsequently arouses the bodhicitta again, and upon hearing the Vaipulya sutras writes them down, yet does not understand them therein.

If one has already resolved upon the Bodhisattva path under ten billion Buddhas, and subsequently again resolves upon the Bodhisattva path, and receives, copies, recites, and reads the Vaipulya sutras, yet is unable to attain the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), nor is able to attain this samādhi, nor takes delight in this samādhi;

whereas if one hears of this samādhi under eighty billion Buddhas, upholds, recites, and reads it, having already resolved upon the Bodhisattva mind before those eighty billion Buddhas, receives the Vaipulya sutras, upholds, copies, recites, and reads them, attains this samādhi, and firmly maintains it—free from blemish and practicing it with devotion—one will ultimately not be seized by Māra, nor be obscured by transgressions.
If one has committed various transgressions throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), those sins shall be eliminated simply by experiencing a headache.

Lacking understanding and meeting with one another, their minds are filled with many anxieties; they are born in lands where kingdoms attack one another,

Regarding what has been taught, they may be suitable for ordinary people but not for elders; furthermore, they are unable to comprehend its meaning, fail to achieve any increase in merit, and frequently fall into fault-finding. If one were to personally perform meritorious deeds before the hands of a hundred Buddhas with a mind free from blemish, at that time [those deeds] would all be ruined and destroyed.

One who acts in this way will swiftly awaken to samādhi.
The radiance of this Wisdom Sūtra is an inexhaustible treasure; abiding in this samādhi, it is beyond counting.
The brilliance of this sūtra surpasses the light of the sun; therefore, by preaching this sūtra, one shall enter the sublime wisdom.
It is like the sun and moon, or the light of various jewel lamps; it is like the winter moon or the snow upon high mountains.

This sutra eliminates the fetters and the transgressions of the mind;
it subdues all Māras, bringing about peace and security.
With supernormal powers and clairvoyance, one gains knowledge of past lives and understands all that people desire.
I recall my past lives: at a time countless eons ago, all craving was completely exhausted, leaving nothing behind.

you shall soon attain [enlightenment] without long delay."

Now, King Kātyāyana, you should receive my instruction: do not engage in worldly conduct like those of the world.

Suppose, for example, that all the people within as many *kṣetra* worlds as there are grains of sand on the banks of the Ganges were to take those very grains of sand and plant them all.

Counting in this manner, planting [the seeds] a thousand times over, and continuing to count in this way until the sands of the Ganges River; counting in such a way,
passing through as many lands as there are grains of sand, taking up a single grain of sand to serve as the unit of calculation.

they should reverently carry out what has been taught above,

It is like a mustard seed beside Mount Sumeru, or like a person drawing a single drop of water from the ocean.

Through the four truths and deliverance, And the wisdom of non-attachment, One can subdue all states of existence;
Without arising or ceasing, Without any fixed location, One can attain purity.
One shall then attain the marks and signs, all meritorious virtues, and the ten powers.
Desiring to understand the subtle and profound dharmas of deep wisdom, one should practice this sutra.
Desiring to understand all those people of the world who have fallen into darkness;
desiring to teach people with truth so as to eliminate their lust and anger and become practitioners of purity—
one should, regarding this sutra, exert oneself day and night to perform the supreme practice.
One should delight in diligence; on the twenty-first day, practice the ritual of the *mudrā-sūtra* without succumbing to indolence, and remain at ease.
Always maintaining gentleness and being free from envy, dwelling in seclusion,
giving the Dharma as a gift, and making offerings through the observance of precepts— one shall thus attain one's wish.
Maintain equanimity and self-restraint, and demonstrate this to all people;
by means of the Samādhi Sūtra, do not delight in sensual desires.
Like a lotus flower that is unstained by water, remain steadfastly established in diligence.
Just as a flying bird, moving through the void, After having traversed this, Then attains the infinite Dhāraṇī-gates.
When this sutra was being preached, three thousand world-systems shook in six ways.

The gods offered hundreds of millions of flowers, incense, music, as well as banners, pennants, silken canopies, jeweled lattices, ornaments of the seven treasures, golden-colored blossoms, mani-jewels, crystal, and lapis lazuli to make offerings to the Buddha.

All the honored devas, celestial maidens, as well as nāgas, ghosts and spirits, asuras, garuḍas, bhikṣus, upāsakas, and upāsikās, were all greatly rejoiced. They all renounced their homes and abandoned all their wives, children, and treasures, giving rise to the bodhicitta. Yet, even if one were to spend one koṭī-nayuta of eons expounding the practice of a bodhisattva, one could not reach its ultimate end.
Those who had conceived the aspiration for bodhicitta all attained the stage of *avaivartika*.
Countless beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all attained the state of *arhat*.
The bodhisattvas from the ten directions who had flown there all departed with joy.
When the Buddha preached this sutra and its Dharma, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) people all resolved their minds toward Bodhisattvahood;
eighty *nayuta* of people all attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*);
and thirty-six million Bodhisattvas attained this samādhi.
Countless people all attained the path of Arhatship.
All the Bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions likewise attained this samādhi.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Bodhisattva King Kāmacintin, Mañjuśrī, the sixty worthies, Queen Bhadrā Śrīṣeṇā of King Bimbisāra, and the devas, humans, nāgas, spirits, and asuras, having heard the sutra, were all greatly rejoiced; they came forward, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
